thread.title: NBS Big 3 upgrade
thread.first_post_html:
My example is from my NBS truck, but this will work for any vehicle. You just have to carefully measure the wire lengths, and figure out how to route the wires.

The purpose of the BIG 3 upgrade is to improve current flow, thus diminishing voltage sag. This is an upgrade/addition to the factory wiring, and not a replacement of the factory wiring. This is not a cure all for dimming headlights, but it's a start. Other recommended upgrades to be used in conjunction with the BIG 3 upgrade are deep cycle batteries (Optima Yellow Top) and high output alternators.

I ended up using some extra 0 gauge wire that I had laying around from previous installs, but 4 gauge will do. For my system, I used Audiopipe battery terminals, Stinger HPM Series 0 gauge (red and silver), and Stinger Expert Series 0 gauge ring terminals.

List of supplies:
1) battery positive to alternator (approx. 4’),
2) battery negative to chassis (approx. 4’),
3) engine block to chassis (approx. 5’),
4) 4 ring terminals,
5) heatshrink (to cover ring terminals),
6) flex loom (I didn’t use any because the Stinger wire was so pretty).

I would estimate the total cost of supplies to be $50-100, depending on the wire size/color and connector type. If you don’t care about how the wire looks, look into using welding wire:

PICS:
The red (+) goes to the alternator +. The silver (-) goes to a chassis bolt under the truck:

The red (+) comes from the battery. The silver (-) is connected to the engine block just above the PS fluid reservoir and goes to a factory ground location on the fire wall:

rewrite.summary: The NBS Big 3 upgrade involves adding thicker wires to improve current flow and reduce voltage sag, which can help with dimming headlights. This is not a replacement of the factory wiring but an addition.
rewrite.rewritten_article_markdown:
The NBS Big 3 upgrade involves adding thicker wires to improve current flow and reduce voltage sag, which can help with dimming headlights. This is not a replacement of the factory wiring but an addition.

This guide will walk you through the necessary components, costs, installation steps, and potential benefits.

### Required Components and Costs
- Battery positive to alternator wire (approx. 4’)
- Battery negative to chassis wire (approx. 4’)
- Engine block to chassis wire (approx. 5’)
- 4 ring terminals
- Heatshrink for covering the ring terminals
- Flex loom (not used in this system, as Stinger wire was sufficient)

Estimated total cost: $50-100, depending on the wire size/color and connector type.

Some users suggest using welding wire, which can be cheaper but may not look as nice.

### Installation Steps
- The red (+) goes to the alternator +. The silver (-) goes to a chassis bolt under the truck.
- The red (+) comes from the battery. The silver (-) is connected to the engine block just above the PS fluid reservoir and goes to a factory ground location on the firewall.

post_rewrites.rewritten_content:
My example uses an NBS truck, but this upgrade applies to any vehicle. Careful measurement and routing of wires are necessary for the BIG 3 upgrade, which aims to improve current flow and reduce voltage sag. This is an addition to factory wiring, not a replacement. It addresses dimming headlights but isn't a comprehensive solution.

Other recommended upgrades include deep cycle batteries (Optima Yellow Top) and high output alternators. I used extra 0 gauge wire from previous installations, though 4 gauge wire would suffice. For my system, I utilized Audiopipe battery terminals, Stinger HPM Series 0 gauge (red and silver), and Stinger Expert Series 0 gauge ring terminals.

Materials needed:
1. Battery positive to alternator (approx. 4')
2. Battery negative to chassis (approx. 4')
3. Engine block to chassis (approx. 5')
4. 4 ring terminals
5. Heatshrink for terminal protection
6. Flex loom (not used due to the Stinger wire quality)

Estimated supply cost: $50-100, depending on wire size/color and connector type.

Wiring connections:
- Red (+) wire goes to the alternator +
- Silver (-) wire connects to a chassis bolt under the truck
- Red (+) comes from the battery
- Silver (-) is connected to the engine block near the power steering fluid reservoir and then to a factory ground on the firewall

[Image: 4/0 welding wire (courtesy of Rick/idbl_Fanatic)]

I haven't confirmed with SPL measurements, but I've noticed that my headlights dim less than stock after this upgrade. Many suggest it's one of the easiest and least expensive electrical upgrades you can make, along with a deep cycle battery like an Optima or a high-output (HO) alternator.

www.weldingsupply.com offers affordable 1/0 wire and terminals; price is the primary factor. Name brand superiority does not justify higher costs in this case. Opt for premium wire if you value appearance, but it won't provide additional functionality. Using Big 3 can effectively address dimming issues at a lower cost.

Originally Posted by snuffalupagis

Total newb question: Are there any downsides to upgrading electrical wires to 0 gauge, especially regarding safety concerns? 

With two out of the three wires being grounds, there are no safety concerns there. The OEM wire from the alternator to the positive terminal of the battery is not fused, so increasing its size would likely make little difference if it shorts. Such a short would require a major front-end collision to occur.

Just completed a major 3-part upgrade, and everything went smoothly with minimal effort. Although I haven’t received my new 200-amp alternator yet, I decided to install the wiring on a nice day. After starting the truck, I noticed the voltage meter reading 13.6 volts instead of the usual 12.3. Adjusting the headunit and shutting off the truck revealed that the subwoofer no longer produced the expected thump. This upgrade seems well worth the time and effort; it took only about an hour to complete.
Could someone provide a clearer explanation of the Big 3? Specifically, what wires are needed and where they should be connected? You mentioned that this is an add-on, not a replacement, correct?

Sure, the Big 3 consist of three essential wires for your setup:

- Battery positive (red wire) to the alternator.
- Battery negative (black wire) to the chassis/frame.
- Engine block to the chassis/frame.

This setup is an addition to your existing wiring and does not replace any components.

Originally Posted by x6369x

Battery positive connected to the alternator, battery negative to the chassis/frame, and engine block also grounded to the chassis/frame. This is an additional setup on top of existing wiring.

For older vehicles, can this new configuration cause any harm?

I plan to keep the positive connection to the starter while adding another to the alternator. While I understand that grounding won’t hurt anything, could you explain exactly what adding the positive connections will accomplish?
Would the stinger side terminals be suitable for replacing the factory wires?
Elemental Designs offers upgrade kits for major audio components. Visit [www.edesignaudio.com/wire_cat.php?catid=48](www.edesignaudio.com/wire_cat.php?catid=48) for more information.

Using stinger side terminals could be a viable option if you want to replace the factory wires. However, since the stock wires are typically bundled within the factory loom with other wires, I do not recommend replacing any of the stock wires unless absolutely necessary.

For older vehicles, adding a positive connection directly to the starter, while keeping grounds intact, could potentially benefit the alternator by providing additional charge. This might improve electrical system performance, enhance gas mileage in newer, computer-driven engines, and reduce the chance of the Check Engine Light (CEL) coming on. It could also bolster the stereo system and extend the life of components.

Battery positive connected to the alternator, battery negative to the chassis/frame, and engine block also grounded to the chassis/frame. This is an addition to the existing wiring.

Do you have any evidence that this upgrade, such as higher voltage readings or improved mileage, actually works? While I am considering trying it, I want to ensure it delivers on its promises before making the change.

You mentioned earlier that you didn't have SPL numbers, but do you have any other evidence showing this upgrade works as intended—such as higher voltage readings or improved mileage? I'm considering trying it, but I want to be sure it performs as expected before doing so. My truck now consistently stays above 10.5 volts instead of dropping to 9 volts, which is a significant improvement for my smaller system.
My car's fuel efficiency has decreased from a hit rate of 11.5 miles per gallon to around 12.8 mpg. Additionally, I'm getting approximately 1.5 extra miles per gallon on the highway.
